changes.detail: A fetch handler's `env` could carry a `Reference` only as a top-level value, so a capability had to be a bare function (`env.query(...)`). An `env` value that is a plain object holding at least one `Reference` now arrives in the isolate as a frozen object of those functions, with any data beside them, so a host can offer `env.database.execute(statement, parameters)` and `env.database.kind`. Each function still calls back to the host as a `Reference` does.
changes.summary: Fetch handler env can hold objects of Reference capabilities

changes.detail: A hardened Worker-backend isolate shared the Worker's real `console`, so sandboxed code could print to the host process's stdout: `console.log` printed even when `onConsole` captured it, uncaptured methods (`info`, `debug`, `dir`, `table`, `trace`) always printed, and Bun's `console.write`, `console._stdout` and `console.Console` wrote there directly. Anything that reads the host's stdout as structured output, such as a log or metering pipeline, could be fed lines that looked like its own. Hardened isolates now get a frozen replacement `console`: `log`, `info` and `debug` go to `onConsole` as `log`, `warn` and `error` keep their level, every other method does nothing, and nothing reaches stdout. Without `onConsole`, output is dropped, as `IsolateOptions.onConsole` always documented. Isolates with `harden: false` keep printing as before.
changes.summary: Sandboxed code can no longer print to the host process's stdout

changes.detail: Bun's browser target quietly replaces `fs`, `path` and other Node built-ins with stubs, so an app that used them bundled cleanly and failed at runtime inside the isolate. `bundleFetchHandler` now refuses them up front: any `node:` or `bun:` import, the `bun` module, a bare Node built-in with no installed npm package of that name (a real `events` or `buffer` package is still fine), and native `.node` addons. It reports every such import at once, with the file that made it, as `FetchHandlerBundleError` (`problems: string[]`). An Elysia 2 app still bundles and runs unchanged.
changes.summary: bundleFetchHandler refuses Bun and Node APIs instead of bundling browser stubs

changes.detail: `createFetchHandler(context, source, options)` loads a Web-standard app (a CommonJS bundle whose default export has `fetch(request, env, ctx)`) into a Worker-backend context and returns a host-side handler: `handler.fetch(request)` copies the request in, rebuilds a `Request` inside the isolate, awaits the app, and returns a host `Response`. `env` takes data and `Reference` capabilities; `ctx.state` persists on the context between requests and is captured by `context.checkpoint({ include: ["state"] })`; `ctx.waitUntil` lets work finish after the response. Bodies are buffered and capped at 1 MiB each way by default (`maxRequestBytes`, `maxResponseBytes`), and `FetchBodyTooLargeError` reports which side overflowed. `handler.fetchWithMetrics` adds the request's run metrics. `bundleFetchHandler(entrypoint)` builds that bundle with `Bun.build`, every dependency inlined, Web APIs only, and `import.meta` defined away. An Elysia 2 app runs through it unchanged.
changes.summary: createFetchHandler and bundleFetchHandler: run fetch(request, env, ctx) apps in an isolate

changes.detail: On the Worker backend, `metrics.cpuMs` was `Date.now()` around the run, so time spent awaiting a host `Reference` or a timer was reported as CPU, rounded to whole milliseconds. It is now the isolate thread's CPU time (user + system, from `process.threadCpuUsage`) at microsecond precision, so a run that waits 300 ms on the host reports under a millisecond of CPU. Two fields are new: `wallMs`, the run's wall-clock duration, and `cpuSource`, `"thread"` when `cpuMs` is thread CPU time or `"wall"` when it is wall time (the FFI backend, or a runtime without `process.threadCpuUsage`). Runs that overlap on one isolate are each charged while they overlap.
changes.summary: metrics.cpuMs is the isolate thread's CPU time, not wall time; adds wallMs and cpuSource

changes.detail: Every Worker-backend isolate checked its heap against `memoryLimit` every 50 ms, idle or not, so a process holding hundreds of idle isolates spent much of a core polling (300 idle isolates: 62% of a core on two cores). The check now runs every 50 ms while the isolate is busy and every second after it has been idle for a second. A host message or a sandboxed timer callback marks it busy and pulls the next check forward, so code that starts allocating after an idle spell is still stopped at the busy rate. 300 idle isolates now take 26% of a core; throughput under load is unchanged.
changes.summary: Idle Worker isolates no longer poll their heap every 50 ms

changes.detail: `IsolateOptions.requireLockdown` and `ResolveIsolatePolicyOverrides.requireLockdown` refuse an unlocked Worker-backend isolate; `ResolvedIsolatePolicy.isolate` can carry it; `Isolate.lockedDown` reports whether this isolate is locked down; `LockdownUnavailableError` (with `reason: "runtime" | "unhardened"`) is what `requireLockdown` throws.

The `ai-tool` and `plugin` policies used to require the FFI backend, so they failed wherever libJavaScriptCore was not installed. They now resolve to `backend: "auto"` with `requireLockdown: true`: FFI when the library is reachable, otherwise a Worker only when the runtime can lock it down, and `LockdownUnavailableError` on a stock Bun without libJavaScriptCore (where they threw `JscLibraryNotFoundError` before). `fallback.allowWorker` is now `true` for both. The `tenant-script` policy is unchanged and leaves `requireLockdown` unset; pass `requireLockdown: true` through `resolveIsolatePolicy` for tenants you do not trust.
changes.summary: ai-tool and plugin policies accept a locked-down Worker when FFI is unavailable

changes.detail: Code running on the Worker backend can load any module through dynamic `import()`, with no eval needed: `import("node:child_process")`, `import("node:fs")` and `import("bun:ffi")` all resolve inside a hardened isolate, on every Bun release up to and including 1.4.4. The `Bun` global also stays reachable through indirect eval and the `Function` constructor, because Bun defines it as non-configurable on Worker globals. Neither can be closed from inside the package. SECURITY.md and the README now say so, and recommend a process, container or microVM boundary around Worker-backend isolates that run code which may try to escape. No code changes.
changes.summary: Documents that the Worker backend does not contain dynamic import() or the Bun global

changes.detail: With `harden` on, the Worker backend now calls `lockdown()` from `bun:jsc` when the running Bun provides it (AbsoluteJS patched Bun 1.4.4+absolute.2 and later). It runs after the worker has loaded what it needs and before any sandboxed code, and it removes the `Bun` global (which hardening cannot delete) and `ShadowRealm`, and makes every `import()` reject. That closes the two paths by which Worker-backend code reached host authority: indirect eval or the `Function` constructor returning `Bun`, and `import("node:child_process")`, `import("node:fs")` or `import("bun:ffi")`. `isolate.lockedDown` reports whether this isolate is locked down (always `true` on the FFI backend), and the new `requireLockdown: true` option throws `LockdownUnavailableError` instead of creating an unlocked Worker-backend isolate. On stock Bun nothing changes unless `requireLockdown` is set.
changes.summary: Worker-backend isolates lock down on patched Bun, closing the Bun-global and import() escapes
